keyVerseText: And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
rootMeaning: The word ὀφείλημα (opheílēma) derives from the root ὀφείλω (opheílō), which conveys the idea of owing or being bound to something, whether pecuniarily or morally. This root emphasizes an obligation or debt that is due, extending beyond mere financial debt to include duties or faults. Thus, ὀφείλημα carries the sense of something owed, not only in a literal sense but also figuratively as a moral or spiritual obligation.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, ὀφείλημα appears only twice, consistently translated as "debt" or "debts," highlighting something owed either materially or figuratively. This limited but focused usage underscores its core meaning as an obligation or liability. The fact that it can refer both to tangible debts and to moral faults reveals its flexibility in capturing the idea of what is due from one person to another or before God.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ὀφείλημα as a debt that encompasses moral faults as well as financial obligations enriches the Christian grasp of sin and forgiveness. Sin is not merely a misstep but a debt owed to God, requiring repayment or pardon. This word reminds believers of their indebtedness to God’s holiness and justice, while also opening the way for grace through forgiveness. Recognizing sin as a debt highlights the necessity of Christ’s atoning work, who pays the ultimate debt on behalf of sinners, freeing them from bondage and restoring their relationship with God.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 6:12, the petition "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" uses ὀφείλημα to express the moral and spiritual debts we owe God and to each other. This word deepens the meaning of forgiveness here, portraying sin as an owed liability that requires release. Asking God to forgive our debts acknowledges our dependence on His mercy, while the parallel call to forgive others reflects the reciprocal nature of grace in the believer’s life.
